notes.meaning: Jeremiah begins by saying that God is always right. Only then does he ask his hard question: why do wicked and two-faced people do so well? He is not picking a fight with God. He wants to understand. When life is confusing, we hold on first to what we know for sure, that the Lord is just.

Jeremiah pictures the wicked as trees that God Himself planted. They have put down roots and are bearing fruit, because God has been kind to them. Yet they only talk about God. Their hearts are far from Him. The old word "reins" (kidneys) stands for a person's deepest feelings. These are hypocrites, people who act religious on the outside but not on the inside.

Unlike those hypocrites, Jeremiah's heart truly belongs to God, and God has tested it and knows it. So he asks God to pull up the wicked like rooted trees. He asks God to lead them off like sheep marked for slaughter. Their long, easy life is like sheep being fattened, and it is getting them ready for judgment.

The land is in drought. The grass is dried up, and even animals and birds are dying because of the people's sin. Jeremiah asks how long this must go on. The people mock him: "He will not see our end." They mean his warnings will never come true. Some older writers take "he" to mean God, as if God did not notice them.

God answers with two sayings. If racing men on foot wears you out, how will you race horses? If you stumble on safe ground, how will you manage in the Jordan thickets where lions live? The trouble from Jeremiah's hometown of Anathoth was small next to what the king, priests and leaders in Jerusalem would do. God gently warns him to get ready for harder trials. Some older interpreters hear these words as aimed at the proud nation, which faced a far worse enemy to come.

Even Jeremiah's own family turned against him. They stirred up a loud crowd after him as if he were a criminal. God tells him not to trust them, even when they speak kindly. Faithful people sometimes find their enemies inside their own home, as Jesus did.

Now God speaks with sorrow. He is leaving His house and His inheritance, His own people, whom He loved like a dear wife. He is handing them over to their enemies. His great love for them shows how ungrateful they were. Being God's people in the past would not shield them from judgment.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars have read verses 7-13 as a lament over a raid that had already happened (2 Kings 24:2), not as a warning about the future.

notes.meaning: God's people, once His gentle sheep, had become like a lion roaring at Him from the forest. They rebelled against Him and raged at His prophets. "I hate her" is strong language for God pulling back His love and protection and letting enemies come.

Other birds often gang up on a bird with strange colors. Judah had become such a "speckled" bird by mixing pagan worship into the worship of God. So the surrounding nations would attack her like birds of prey. God calls the wild beasts, meaning enemy armies, to come and devour.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some translators, following the ancient Greek version, read the word as "hyena" rather than "speckled bird."

notes.meaning: The "shepherds" are the Babylonian generals and kings. They bring their armies like flocks that eat up and trample a vineyard. Even now God tenderly calls the land "My vineyard" and "My pleasant field." Yet it will become a wasteland.
The ruined land seems to mourn before God. Yet the people do not take it to heart. They do not see these troubles as God's judgment, and they do not turn back to Him in sorrow and prayer.

The invaders will reach even the bare hills and lonely pasture lands. No place is safe. It is called "the sword of the LORD" because God is using the enemy army to judge His people. The prophet speaks of the future as if it had already happened, because it is so sure.

The people worked hard and expected a good harvest, but they got thorns instead. Their plans, their alliances and their money would not save them. Without turning back to God, all their efforts would end in shame.

God turns to Judah's "evil neighbors": Edom, Moab, Ammon and others who attacked His people. He will uproot them from their own land. He will also pull Judah out from among them, rescuing those who had been taken captive or had fled there. God still keeps His promise to His people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars have thought verses 14-17 were a separate message given at a later time.

notes.meaning: Surprisingly, God promises mercy even to these enemy nations. After punishing them, He will have compassion and bring each people back to its own land. God's anger is not endless, even toward outsiders.

The nations that once taught Israel to swear by the false god Baal are invited to learn God's ways instead. To swear "As surely as the LORD lives" means to honor and worship the true God alone. If they do, they will be "built" among God's people as full members. This came true in part after the exile, and more fully when non-Jews came to faith in Christ.

The offer has a serious other side. Any nation that refuses to obey will be uprooted for good. Those who will not be led by God's grace will face His justice. The warning was also meant for Judah, who knew God's law and had even less excuse.
